Distress
dih-STRES
n.
From Old French destresse, “narrowness, anguish,” from Latin distringere, “to draw apart, hinder.” Renders the Hebrew tsarāh, “narrowness, distress,” from tsar (narrow), and the Greek thlipsis, “pressure, affliction.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Distress in Scripture is the soul’s tight, pressed-in condition under affliction—the narrow place from which the saint cries to the LORD and out of which the LORD characteristically delivers His people. The Hebrew imagery is geometric: tsarāh from tsar (narrow) pictures the saint constricted, hemmed in, with no room to maneuver. The Greek thlipsis picks up the same image: pressure, tribulation, the inward squeeze of outward affliction. The Psalter is saturated with the verb-pair of distress and deliverance: I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place; then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he saved them out of their distresses (a refrain repeated four times in Ps 107); thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Paul gathers the same theology under the New Testament: who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. The biblical pattern of distress has therefore four marks. First, it is real: Scripture does not pretend the saint will be exempt from the tight places, the constricting providences, the pressure that bears in on body and soul. Second, it is the appointed setting in which the soul’s cry rises and the LORD’s deliverance is wrought: before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word; the very narrowness of the distress is the setting in which God’s salvation is most vividly known. Third, it does not separate the saint from the love of Christ; the apostle’s comprehensive list (Rom 8:35) is given precisely to show that no distress, however severe, can cut the bond. Fourth, it is the present antechamber to glory: I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us; and Christ’s own promise in John 16:33: in the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world. The biblical disposition under distress is therefore neither denial nor despair but the cry of the saint who knows the LORD’s habit—and waits, even in the narrowest place, for the deliverance the LORD characteristically works for those who call upon Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DISTRESS as extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; severe affliction; calamity; the act of distraining; in scripture, the constricted condition of the soul under affliction, set against the LORD’s characteristic deliverance.

expand to see more

DISTRESS, n. — 1. The act of distraining; the taking of any personal chattel from a wrong-doer, to procure satisfaction. 2. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind. 3. The cause of pain or anguish; affliction; calamity. 4. A state of danger or extreme need, in which we have no resource. I will save them from all their distresses (Ezek 37:23).

DISTRESSED, pp. or a. — Suffering great pain or torture; harassed; afflicted with calamity; oppressed with want.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 120:1 — "In my distress I cried unto the LORD, and he heard me."

Psalm 107:6 — "Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses."

Romans 8:35 — "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"

John 16:33 — "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Distress is corrupted, on one side, by the prosperity-and-comfort register that treats every tight place as evidence of God’s absence or the saint’s insufficient faith—and on the other by the stoic register that minimizes distress as unworthy of expression, against the Psalter’s candid cries and Christ’s own tears.

expand to see more

The prosperity-and-comfort register reads every distress as evidence of God’s absence or the saint’s insufficient faith—the believer is told that the LORD wants him in the large place, never in the narrow, and that the persistence of distress in his life means something is wrong with his praying, his believing, or his obedience. Scripture refuses the reading. The Psalter is saturated with distress; the apostle’s catalog in 2 Corinthians 11 lists his own distresses at length; Christ Himself in Gethsemane was exceeding sorrowful, even unto death; the saints of Hebrews 11 were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, slain with the sword. Distress is the regular setting of the Christian life in this present age, and the LORD’s characteristic deliverance is wrought precisely in and through the distress, not by exempting the saint from it. Recover the doctrine, and the saint stops reading every tight place as evidence of divine displeasure and begins reading it as the appointed antechamber in which the cry rises and the deliverance is wrought.

The opposite corruption is the stoic register that minimizes distress as unworthy of expression, requires the saint to perform a composure he does not feel, and reads the Psalmist’s tearful complaints as a lower spirituality the mature believer has transcended. The Psalter and Christ’s own example refuse this. The Psalmist cries, complains, weeps, asks how long?—and the Spirit included his complaint in the inspired hymnal of the church. Christ wept at Lazarus’s tomb, sweat as it were great drops of blood in Gethsemane, cried with a loud voice on the cross. The expression of distress before God is biblically authorized; the suppression of it as a token of strength is not the higher spirituality but a lower one. Recover both ends. Refuse the prosperity reading that treats distress as evidence of divine absence, and refuse the stoic reading that requires its suppression—and the saint can bring his actual distress to the actual LORD who has the actual habit of delivering His people out of their distresses, characteristically in His time and in His way.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsarāh (narrowness, distress) from tsar (narrow); Greek thlipsis (pressure, affliction)—the soul’s tight, pressed-in condition under affliction, set against the LORD’s characteristic deliverance and the love of Christ from which it cannot separate the saint.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsarāh (H6869) — distress, trouble (the “narrowness” word; Ps 9:9; 22:11; 50:15; 119:143).

Hebrew tsar (H6862) — narrow, tight; the geometric root of distress imagery.

Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation (the great NT distress word).

Greek stenōchōria (G4730) — narrowness of place, anguish (Rom 8:35; 2 Cor 6:4).

Usage

"I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place—the saint’s characteristic experience and the LORD’s characteristic answer."

"Distress is the appointed antechamber in which the soul’s cry rises and the LORD’s salvation is most vividly known."

"Prosperity reading treats distress as divine absence; stoic reading treats it as unworthy of expression; biblical pattern brings the actual distress to the actual LORD who actually delivers."
